title: Serving the sick
hookLine: whoever would care for me, let him care for the sick
tomorrow: why did the Buddha make a rule about cutting trees?

lines: A MONK NO ONE WOULD TEND.
cards: A room with someone sick in it has a smell: cough drops, a trash can of tissues, air that hasn't moved. Jess, Mai's roommate, has been in bed with a fever for two days, and Mai has been sketching in the hallway.
The Vinaya tells of a room much worse. A monk lies sick with dysentery, fallen in his own filth, and no one is tending him. Then the Buddha, walking through the lodgings with Ananda, finds him.

teach.h: "IS THERE NO ONE TO LOOK AFTER YOU?"
teach.b: He asks: what's wrong with you, monk? Dysentery. Is there no one looking after you?
No, the monk says. I'm of no use to the others, so they don't. The Buddha doesn't call a meeting first.

teach.h: WATER POURED, A BODY WASHED AND LIFTED.
teach.b: He sends Ananda for water. He pours, and Ananda washes. Then, together, the Buddha at the head and Ananda at the feet, they lift the monk onto a bed.
Only after that does he gather the monks and ask the hard question. You have no mother here, no father to nurse you.
If you don't nurse one another, who will?

teach.h: CARE FOR ME: CARE FOR THE SICK.
teach.b: Then the line: whoever would care for me, let him care for the sick.
That's why nursing the sick became a duty in the monks' own rule, and why Buddhists sit by hospital beds to chant, cook for families with someone ill, and keep company with the dying.

Listen to the senses in the story: water, a smell no one wanted, two pairs of hands, the weight of a body lifted. The teaching is in that weight. Caring for the sick is caring for the Buddha, in his own words.

how: Buddhist monastic rules make nursing a sick monk a duty of his companions; lay Buddhists visit and cook for the sick, invite monks to chant for them, and sit with the dying, often chanting quietly at the bedside.

o: a rule keeping sick monks apart from healthy ones
praying for the sick from a distance, never visiting
caring for the ill as if caring for the Buddha himself

games.q: the room no one would enter — tap the pairs.
p: "I'm of no use to the others"
poured the water, lifted his head

s: the Buddha told other monks to clean the sick monk while he watched
he poured the water himself while Ananda washed, and they lifted him together.
the sick monk said no one tended him because he was no use to them
that's his answer when the Buddha asks if anyone is looking after him.
in Buddhism, nursing the sick is a job for lay people, not monks
the Buddha made it a duty among the monks themselves.

games.q: a woman from your grandmother's temple is sick at home, and you're asked to drop off soup. you're nervous about seeing someone ill. what fits the Vinaya story?
o: go in, set it down, and sit with her for a few minutes
leave it on the porch; a sick person wants to be left alone
send money for takeout instead; the thought is what counts
games.why: the Buddha didn't send help from a distance. he went into the room, poured the water and lifted. presence is the care.

practice: If water is near, pour a little over your hands, slowly, and feel its warmth or cool, its weight. Think of whoever is sick in your life right now, near or far. Dry your hands, and let them rest open on your knees through the sit.

wordCard.voice: Serving the sick: water, hands, and the weight of a body lifted, because the Buddha said that's how you care for him.

orig.note: Pali: a sick person; the Vinaya's word for the monk no one tended.

carryVoice: Keep this: care for the sick, and by his own words you've cared for the Buddha. Twenty-two days in the block.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII.26 (the monk sick with dysentery)
